literal:
The Book of Generations

Genesis 5 opens with a solemn declaration: "This is the book of the generation of Adam" (Gen 5:1). The Hebrew term sefer toledoth (book of generations) marks this as an official genealogical record, connecting the creation account to the subsequent history of humanity. This is one of several toledoth sections that structure Genesis as a whole.

The Righteous Line of Seth

St. Augustine, in City of God Book XV, explains that this genealogy traces the "City of God" through Seth's line, in contrast to Cain's descendants who represent the earthly city. After Abel's death, "the generations diverge, the one branch deriving from Cain, the other from him whom Adam begot in the room of Abel slain by his brother, and whom he called Seth." These two lines "represent the two cities in their distinctive ranks, the one the heavenly city, which sojourns on earth, the other the earthly, which gapes after earthly joys."

Didymus the Blind explains why the genealogy begins with Seth rather than Cain or Abel: "Seth was the third, not the first, to be born, it should be said in reply that it was not proper to begin with Cain, criminal as he was, nor with Abel, who died childless, but rather as a result with Seth, who in a sense was firstborn."

Adam's Image in Seth

Genesis 5:3 states that Adam "begot a son in his own likeness, after his image, and called his name Seth." St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis (Homily 21), interprets this: "Scripture does not speak here of the features of the body, when it says: In its image and likeness, but in the qualities of the soul, so that we may understand that it will not resemble Cain." Chrysostom emphasizes that nothing in Scripture is left to chance: "Adam, he says, engendered such an image and likeness, and named it Seth"—meaning Seth preserved "the same stamp of virtue, revealing the image of his father in his actions."

The Long Lifespans

The patriarchs lived extraordinarily long lives: Adam 930 years, Seth 912, Enos 905, Cainan 910, Malaleel 895, Jared 962, Mathusala 969 (the longest), Lamech 777, and Noah 950. Augustine addressed these remarkable ages in City of God, affirming: "On the basis of Sacred Scripture, however, we calculate that not even six thousand years have passed since the origin of mankind." He took the genealogical numbers as literal chronologies, defending the historical accuracy of the pre-flood patriarchs' long lives.

Augustine also noted textual variations: "The question arises because of the poor preservation of the manuscripts, for not only the Hebrew manuscripts contain different numbers, but some manuscripts of the Septuagint... say Methuselah died six years before the flood." St. Jerome discussed "a famous question, agitated and discussed in all churches" regarding calculations that seem to place Methuselah's death after the flood.

The Significance of Names

Some scholars interpret Mathusala (Methuselah) as meaning "when he dies, it shall come," suggesting a prophetic dimension to his name. According to ancient chronologies, Methuselah died in the very year of the Flood, possibly indicating that his name prophesied the coming judgment. The apocryphal writer Eupolemus affirms that Enoch, being a prophet, gave his son this name under a spirit of prophecy, foretelling when the flood would come.

The Refrain of Death

The chapter's literary structure emphasizes mortality through the repeated refrain: "and he died." For each patriarch, Scripture records his years, his offspring, and then the final verdict: "and he died." This solemn repetition underscores the reality of death as the consequence of Adam's sin (Gen 2:17, Rom 5:12). The genealogy serves as a record not merely of life but of the universal reign of death.

The Exception: Enoch

In the midst of this litany of death stands one remarkable exception: Enoch, who "walked with God, and was seen no more, because God took him" (Gen 5:24). The Septuagint renders "walked with God" as "was well-pleasing to God," which the Epistle to the Hebrews quotes: "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death" (Heb 11:5). Enoch lived 365 years—notably the number of days in a solar year—and his translation breaks the pattern of death that dominates this chapter.
allegorical:
The Genealogy Leading to Christ

St. Luke's Gospel traces Christ's genealogy from Jesus back through David, Abraham, and ultimately to "Adam, who was of God" (Lk 3:23-38). This genealogy passes through every patriarch named in Genesis 5: Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared, Enoch, Mathusala, Lamech, and Noah. The "book of the generation of Adam" thus becomes the opening chapter of what will culminate in the New Adam, Christ.

While Matthew's genealogy presents Jesus as the Son of David and Son of Abraham, emphasizing his Jewish kingship, Luke's genealogy "presents Jesus as the second Adam, a son of God." Luke moves from Jesus' baptism and his genealogy to his temptation, presenting his readers with the question: "Will this New Man succeed where all the others have failed?"

Seth as Type of Christ

Augustine identifies Seth with resurrection hope. Eve named him Seth ("appointed" or "substitute") because "God has raised me up another seed for Abel whom Cain slew" (Gen 4:25). Seth represents "the new birth of a race of men who are tied to God"—a prefigurement of Christ who, as the true "seed," would replace what was lost through sin. As Abel died innocently at his brother's hand, so Christ would die; as Seth was raised up to continue the promised line, so Christ would rise.

Enoch as Type of Christ's Ascension

Enoch's translation without seeing death prefigures Christ's Ascension. St. Ephrem the Syrian suggested that God transported Enoch to Paradise while Adam was still alive, "so that Adam might be comforted by this righteous descendant and know that Paradise would be the meeting place for all who were like Enoch." Just as Enoch was taken bodily to God's presence, so Christ ascended bodily to the right hand of the Father.

The Epistle to the Hebrews draws the allegorical connection explicitly: "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death... for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God" (Heb 11:5). Christ is the one who supremely "pleased God" (cf. Mt 3:17), and who has entered heaven itself to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.

Enoch and Elijah: Types of the Assumption

Catholic tradition sees in Enoch's translation a type of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Just as Enoch "walked with God" and was taken up without experiencing death, so Mary, who bore God incarnate and remained ever-faithful, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. The Catechism affirms that intimate communion with God is humanity's true destiny.

The Two Witnesses

A strong patristic tradition identifies Enoch and Elijah as the "two witnesses" of Revelation 11 who will return at the end of time. St. Irenaeus wrote in Adversus Haereses (Book IV, Chapter 30): "The disciples of the Apostles say that they (Enoch and Elijah) whose living bodies were taken up from the earth, have been placed in an earthly paradise, where they will remain until the end of the world."

Tertullian affirmed: "Enoch no doubt was translated, and so was Elijah; nor did they experience death: it was postponed, and only postponed, most certainly: they are reserved for the suffering of death, that by their blood they may extinguish Antichrist." Hippolytus wrote: "In that week, the two prophets, Enoch and Elijah, will take up the half. For they will preach 1260 days clothed in sackcloth, proclaiming repentance to the people and to all the nations."

St. Thomas Aquinas later affirmed: "Elijah was raised into the aerial, not the empyrean heaven, which is the abode of the Saints, and in like manner Enoch was carried away to a terrestrial paradise, where he and Elijah, it is believed, will live together until the coming of the Antichrist."

Noah as Type of Christ and the Ark as Church

The genealogy culminates in Noah, whose very name means "rest" or "comfort." Lamech prophesied at his birth: "This same shall comfort us" (Gen 5:29). The Church Fathers consistently interpreted Noah as a type of Christ: "In the Fathers and tradition, Noah is considered as the type and figure of the Saviour, because through him the human race was saved from destruction and reconciled with God. As he built the ark, the only means of salvation from the Deluge, so Christ established the Church, the only means of salvation in the spiritual order."
moral:
Walking with God

The phrase "walked with God" appears twice for Enoch (Gen 5:22, 24) and once for Noah (Gen 6:9), setting these two patriarchs apart from all others in the pre-flood world. To "walk with God" means to make a relationship with God part of one's everyday lifestyle, to honor God in every aspect of life. Genesis emphasizes that Enoch "walked with God for three hundred years," indicating not a momentary conversion but a sustained and habitual life of holiness.

The moral lesson is clear: faithfulness is not measured by dramatic moments but by persistent, daily communion with God. Enoch's walk lasted centuries, through the births of children and grandchildren, through the ordinary rhythms of life. His holiness was worked out in the midst of a corrupt generation (cf. Gen 6:5), demonstrating that fidelity to God is possible even when surrounded by wickedness.

The Reality of Death

The repeated refrain "and he died" confronts the reader with mortality's inescapable reality. No matter how long these patriarchs lived—Adam 930 years, Mathusala 969—death claimed them all. This sobering repetition teaches that length of days does not confer immunity from death, that even the most blessed and long-lived must face the end.

The moral application is profound: we must live with eternity in view. The Psalmist prays, "Teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Ps 90:12). Genesis 5 numbers the days of the patriarchs precisely so that we might learn that our days too are numbered. Death is not distant but certain, and wisdom lies in preparing for it through holy living.

Faithfulness Across Generations

The genealogy emphasizes not just individuals but generations. Each patriarch "begot sons and daughters," transmitting the faith to future generations. Seth preserved Adam's likeness, and his descendants preserved the worship of the true God while Cain's line descended into violence and pride (Gen 4:17-24).

St. John Chrysostom noted that Eve attributed Seth not "to nature nor to childbirth... but to the virtue of God." The moral lesson for parents and grandparents is to raise children who preserve the stamp of virtue, who reveal the image of their spiritual fathers in their actions. Faith must be handed down, consciously and deliberately, from generation to generation.

The Danger of Compromise

The genealogy leads to a warning: Genesis 6 will reveal that "the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives" (Gen 6:2). Augustine believed that this refers to the intermarriage between Seth's righteous line and Cain's corrupt line, which led to the degradation of humanity before the Flood. The moral lesson is vigilance against compromise with worldliness, against alliances that draw believers away from faithful living.

Pleasing God

The Septuagint renders Enoch's "walking with God" as being "well-pleasing to God," a phrase the Epistle to the Hebrews quotes (Heb 11:5). The author of Hebrews then adds: "Without faith it is impossible to please God" (Heb 11:6). Enoch's example teaches that the foundation of the moral life is faith—trust in God that leads to obedient action.

Enoch "obtained the witness that before his translation he was pleasing to God." This "witness" or testimony came before his reward. The moral order is clear: first faithful living, then divine approval, then reward. Enoch did not seek translation; he sought to please God, and God honored that seeking.
anagogical:
Enoch's Translation: Hope of Resurrection

Enoch's bodily assumption into God's presence without experiencing death offers the first scriptural indication that death is not the final word. The Church teaches that Enoch's translation "prefigures later assumptions and confirms that death is not intrinsic to human nature but a consequence of sin." If death came through Adam's sin (Rom 5:12), then bodily assumption into glory reveals what humanity was always meant for.

The Epistle to the Hebrews interprets Enoch's translation as a reward of faith: "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death" (Heb 11:5). This points forward to the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting. What was granted to Enoch as a singular privilege will be granted to all the faithful at the Last Day.

Those Who Will Not Sleep

St. Paul teaches that at Christ's return, "we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet" (1 Cor 15:51-52). Typologically, Enoch prefigures those who will be transformed at the Second Coming without passing through death. His translation anticipates the "rapture" of the living saints, who "shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thess 4:17).

Paradise Regained

St. Ephrem the Syrian suggested that Enoch was transported to the earthly Paradise, the garden from which Adam and Eve were expelled. This interpretation points toward the anagogical hope: Paradise lost through Adam will be Paradise regained through Christ. Enoch's dwelling in Paradise prefigures the return of the faithful to communion with God in the new creation.

The apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus records Enoch saying: "I am Enoch, who was translated by the word of God... Here we have hitherto been, and have not tasted death, but are now about to return at the coming of Antichrist." Whether understood as earthly paradise or heavenly glory, Enoch's destination represents the eschatological hope of all believers.

The New Creation Through Noah

The genealogy culminates in Noah, through whom humanity will be saved from destruction and given a new beginning. Noah's flood represents a type of baptism (1 Pet 3:20-21), and the post-flood world represents a kind of new creation. But the fullness of new creation awaits the end of history, when "there shall be a new heaven and a new earth" (Rev 21:1).

The progression from Adam through the patriarchs to Noah, and from Noah through subsequent generations to Christ, reveals God's patient work of salvation across millennia. The anagogical sense sees this history as directed toward its final goal: the restoration of all things in Christ (Acts 3:21), when death itself will be destroyed and God will be "all in all" (1 Cor 15:28).

The Communion of Saints

Origen, Athanasius, and Chrysostom mention a tradition that Adam was buried at Golgotha, the very place where Christ would be crucified. Whether historical or symbolic, this tradition unites the first Adam with the last Adam (1 Cor 15:45), suggesting that redemption touches the very origins of humanity. The anagogical sense points to the communion of saints, where all the patriarchs of Genesis 5 now rejoice in the presence of God alongside all who have died in faith.

The "book of the generation of Adam" is not merely ancient history but an ongoing story that encompasses all the faithful, from Abel to the last saint who will enter glory. As the patriarchs awaited the promises from afar (Heb 11:13), so we await the final fulfillment when "we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2).
